newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Kabila to take office with sweeping powers.
newsitem.headline: Kabila to take office with sweeping powers.

text.p: Self-proclaimed president Laurent Kabila, whose forces drove veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko from power in a seven-month civil war, takes office as head of state on Thursday at Kinshasa's main sports stadium.

State radio declared Thursday a public holiday in the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, former Zaire, and broadcast repeated messages urging the population to turn out in force for the inauguration ceremony.
"Today is an historic day for our country," it said. "All Kinois (Kinshasa citizens) are requested to turn out at the stadium for the investiture," it said.
The stadium, formerly named Kamanyola after Mobutu's most famous battle, had been renamed the Martyrs Stadium, it added.

Kabila's, whose forces marched into Kinshasa on May 17, on Wednesday decreed himself sweeping powers to run the country until the adoption of a new transitional constitution by a promised constituent council.
Earlier, his soldiers broke up a third opposition protest in under a week.
Wednesday's 15-article decree, broadcast on state radio and television, said the nation's three institutions were the president, the government and the judiciary.
The judiciary would remain independent and individual liberties would be guaranteed subject to respect of the law, public order and morals, it added.
"The government conducts the policies of the nation as defined by the president," the decree said.
The president has the power to hire and fire members of the government and, after consultation, other holders of state posts, including in the judiciary and the armed forces.
Mobutu ruled mineral-rich Zaire for over three decades, during which rampant corruption and administrative chaos drained what is potentially one of Africa's richest nations.
Foreign and domestic pressure forced him to abandon his near absolute powers in 1990 for a democratic transition but implementation dragged.
Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo has banned political activity and public demonstrations, citing the need to preserve public order.

Several thousand supporters of Etienne Tshisekedi, a veteran Mobutu opponent, took part in Wednesday's march, denouncing the continued presence in Kinshasa of Rwandans among Kabila's forces and seeking power-sharing.

Kabila has set up a 13-member government. Aides say he plans to name seven more ministers but not a prime minister, the post Tshisekedi claims is constitutionally his after a 1992 national conference vote under Zaire's democratic transition.

Tshisekedi enjoys support in the capital's poor districts. His Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) has called another march for Friday. State radio announced a parallel march by supporters of Kabila.
Soldiers from Kabila's Alliance allowed Wednesday's march to go ahead but dispersed the protesters later, firing in the air and beating them with batons and rifle butts.
"We will continue until there is an army in the service of the people," Tshisekedi ally Joseph Olenghankoy said, but he expressed the hope that Tshisekedi and Kabila would meet.
Oleghankoy said at least 30 protesters were arrested.
Opposition activists marched in Kinshasa last Friday and Saturday before the ban. Soldiers broke up those marches.

At the United Nations, diplomats said envoys from at least a dozen countries planned to tell Kabila face-to-face he must do something about human rights and the treatment of Rwandan refugees in his country.

A group of 21 ambassadors, including those from the United States, European states, Canada, Japan, Egypt and South Africa, met after senior U.N. officials asked them to consider what they could do to express their concerns.

Many said their governments would probably send their Kinshasa ambassadors in one large group to see Kabila before he leaves for the Organisation of African Unity summit in the Zimbabwean capital Harare this weekend.
